relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls how a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque that proved genuine. Enfield names him Hyde, deformed and detestable, still holding the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

[P35] “Have you any of these papers?” asked Mr. Utterson.
[P36] Poole felt in his pocket and handed out a crumpled note, which the lawyer, bending nearer to the candle, carefully examined. Its contents ran thus: “Dr. Jekyll presents his compliments to Messrs. Maw. He assures them that their last sample is impure and quite useless for his present purpose. In the year 18—, Dr. J. purchased a somewhat large quantity from Messrs. M. He now begs them to search with most sedulous care, and should any of the same quality be left, forward it to him at once. Expense is no consideration. The importance of this to Dr. J. can hardly be exaggerated.” So far the letter had run composedly enough, but here with a sudden splutter of the pen, the writer’s emotion had broken loose. “For God’s sake,” he added, “find me some of the old.”
[P37] “This is a strange note,” said Mr. Utterson; and then sharply, “How do you come to have it open?”
[P38] “The man at Maw’s was main angry, sir, and he threw it back to me like so much dirt,” returned Poole.
[P39] “This is unquestionably the doctor’s hand, do you know?” resumed the lawyer.
[P40] “I thought it looked like it,” said the servant rather sulkily; and then, with another voice, “But what matters hand of write?” he said. “I’ve seen him!”
[P41] “Seen him?” repeated Mr. Utterson. “Well?”

known_before.name: Poole
known_before.tagline: Elderly servant at Dr. Jekyll's house
known_before.bio: Poole is the elderly servant at Dr. Jekyll's house, obedient to his master and to Hyde as his superior. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, confirmed Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, said all servants had orders to obey Hyde, and that Hyde never dined there and mostly used the laboratory. He admitted Utterson to Jekyll's cabinet and told him no letter came except by post. He reported that Jekyll had shut his door against Utterson and was confined. Utterson now prefers speaking with Poole

known_before.tagline: Tramples a girl, pays with a cheque
known_before.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, the favourite of Jekyll, and the heir named in Jekyll's will. He is merciless, inspires enduring hatred, and impresses beholders with a sense of unexpressed deformity. He trampled over a girl's body and left her screaming, was forced by threats of scandal to pay a hundred pounds, and led Enfield's group to a door where he returned with gold and a cheque. He later met Utterson at that door, gave his address in Soho, angrily accused Utterson of lying
